data.rationale: Tile the outer row loop (M=64) into chunks of 32. With 30 SMs on Ampere, 64/32=2 tiles — each tile covers 32 rows, keeping 2 concurrent waves across SMs. This exposes enough parallelism without over-fragmenting work, and aligns well to warp-multiple boundaries.

Tile the inner reduction loop (N=2048) into chunks of 1024. This splits the 2048-element reduction into two phases of 1024 elements each, fitting comfortably in the 49152 bytes of shared memory (1024 * 4 bytes = 4KB per row tile), enabling staged two-pass mean+variance computation with good register reuse.

Map each row (i) to a distinct thread block (threadblock.x). LayerNorm is embarrassingly parallel across rows — each row is independent. With M=64 rows and 30 SMs, this gives ~2 waves of 32 blocks each, saturating the GPU. This is the canonical high-performance layernorm pattern: one CTA per row handles the full reduction over N=2048.

Vectorize the inner j-loop with width 4 (float4 / 128-bit loads). N=2048 is divisible by 4, enabling coalesced 128-bit memory transactions. This reduces the number of memory instructions by 4×, maximizing memory bandwidth utilization on Ampere's L2/HBM. Width-4 is the sweet spot for FP32 (4×4B = 16B = 128-bit, matching cache line granularity).
